parts.stem: Name the four concurrent lines passing through the point $M$ in the diagram.

steps.explain: We start by identifying the point \(M\) in the diagram, which is the red dot in the center. We need to identify all distinct lines that pass through this single intersection point.
steps.work: \( \text{Point } M \text{ is the point of concurrency} \)

steps.explain: Next, we trace the straight lines passing directly through \(M\). By observing the labeled points, the horizontal line is line \(AB\), the vertical line is line \(CD\), and we also have two diagonal lines which are named \(EF\) and \(GH\).
Finally, we combine these names to identify the matching option. The correct list containing all four straight lines passing through \(M\) is Lines \(AB\), \(CD\), \(EF\), and \(GH\).
steps.work: \( \text{Final Answer: Lines } AB, \; CD, \; EF, \; GH \)

parts.stem: Name the two parallel lines, using the correct symbol for "is parallel to".

steps.explain: We begin by locating the parallel lines in the geometry diagram. Parallel lines are represented visually with matching arrows or arrowheads pointing in the same direction.
steps.work: \( \text{Look for matching blue dashed lines with arrowheads} \)

steps.explain: Next, we observe that the left vertical dashed line passes through points \(A\) and \(C\) (line \(AC\)), and the right vertical dashed line passes through points \(B\) and \(D\) (line \(BD\)).
Finally, we apply the standard parallel notation symbol \(\\parallel\). Writing that line \(AC\) is parallel to line \(BD\) yields \(AC \\parallel BD\).

parts.stem: Name the point of intersection of the lines $AB$ and $CD$.

steps.explain: We start by identifying the two lines \(AB\) (the horizontal line) and \(CD\) (the vertical solid line) on the coordinate plane.
Next, we trace both lines to locate the single point where they cross each other. This is the intersection point.
Finally, we read the label of this intersection point from the diagram, which is clearly marked as \(M\). Thus, the correct option is Point \(M\).

parts.stem: Name the line joining $C$ and the intersection of $AB$ and $CD$.

steps.explain: We begin by determining the intersection of lines \(AB\) and \(CD\), which we previously found to be the point \(M\).
Next, we identify the line that connects point \(C\) and this intersection point \(M\).
Finally, in standard geometric notation, a line passing through points \(C\) and \(M\) is named Line \(CM\). This corresponds directly to our correct option.

parts.stem: What point belongs to both lines $AC$ and $CD$?

steps.explain: We start by identifying the two lines \(AC\) (the left dashed vertical line) and \(CD\) (the vertical solid line passing through the center).
Next, we find the common point shared by both lines. This is the point of intersection between line \(AC\) and line \(CD\).
Finally, looking at the letter designations, both lines share the letter \(C\). The intersection point in the diagram is Point \(C\).

parts.stem: In symbols, write "$WX$ is parallel to $ZY$".

steps.explain: We begin by identifying the two lines to compare: Line \(WX\) (the top horizontal line) and Line \(ZY\) (the bottom horizontal line).
Next, we recall that the standard mathematical symbol for representing that two lines are parallel (never intersecting in the same plane) is \(\\parallel\).
Finally, we combine the line names with the parallel symbol to write \(WX \\parallel ZY\). This matches option A.

parts.stem: In symbols, write "$XY$ is parallel to $WZ$".

steps.explain: We begin by locating the two slanted parallel lines in the diagram: Line \(XY\) on the right and Line \(WZ\) on the left.
Next, we use the standard parallel operator \(\\parallel\) to represent that these two lines have the same slope and will never cross.
Finally, we write the symbolic expression representing this relationship, which is \(XY \\parallel WZ\). This corresponds directly to option A.

parts.stem: What is the intersection of the lines $WX$ and $XY$?

steps.explain: We begin by identifying the two lines to intersect: Line \(WX\) (the top horizontal line) and Line \(XY\) (the right slanted line).
Next, we find the common letter/point between the names of the two lines, which represents the point where they cross each other in the diagram.
Finally, looking at the diagram, the two lines meet at the top-right corner, which is labeled Point \(X\). Thus, the correct option is Point \(X\).

parts.stem: What point lies on both $XY$ and $YZ$?

steps.explain: We start by identifying the two lines in question: Line \(XY\) (the right slanted line) and Line \(YZ\) (the bottom horizontal line).
Next, we look for the common point shared by both lines. Mathematically, this is their point of intersection.
Finally, observing the letters, both names share the letter \(Y\). Looking at the diagram, the bottom-right corner where they meet is Point \(Y\).

parts.stem: Do any points lie on both lines $WX$ and $ZY$?
options: No, because parallel lines never intersect.

steps.explain: We begin by locating lines \(WX\) (top horizontal line) and \(ZY\) (bottom horizontal line) in the diagram.
Next, we observe that these two lines are parallel to each other. By definition, parallel lines in the same plane never meet, no matter how far they are extended.
Finally, since they never intersect, there are no common points between them. Therefore, the correct answer is: No, because parallel lines never intersect.

parts.stem: According to Pappus' Theorem, what special mathematical property is shared by points $X, Y,$ and $Z$?
options: They are collinear (they lie on a single straight line)
They are concurrent (lines pass through them)
They are perpendicular to each other

steps.explain: We start by identifying the three cross-intersection points in the diagram: Point \(X\) (intersection of \(DV\) and \(UE\)), Point \(Y\) (intersection of \(EW\) and \(VF\)), and Point \(Z\) (intersection of \(FU\) and \(WD\)).
steps.work: \( X = DV \\cap UE, \; Y = EW \\cap VF, \; Z = FU \\cap WD \)

steps.explain: Next, we observe the blue dashed line passing horizontally through the center of the figure. Point \(X\), Point \(Z\), and Point \(Y\) all lie directly on this single straight line.
Finally, we recall that the geometric property of points lying on a single straight line is called collinearity. Therefore, according to Pappus' Theorem, points \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) are collinear.

parts.stem: If you construct the lines $PQ$ and $SR$, and produce (extend) them, at which point do they meet?

steps.explain: We begin by locating points \(P, Q, S,\) and \(R\) representing the vertices of the general quadrangle in the diagram. We identify the side lines \(PQ\) and \(SR\).
Next, we extend (produce) both of these lines in the direction of their convergence until they meet.
Finally, tracing the extended lines, they intersect at the far right point labeled as Point \(X\). This matches option A.

parts.stem: If you construct the lines $PS$ and $QR$, and produce (extend) them, at which point do they meet?

steps.explain: We begin by identifying the other pair of opposite sides in the quadrangle: Line \(PS\) (left side) and Line \(QR\) (right side).
Next, we extend both lines upwards towards their point of convergence.
Finally, tracing the extensions of \(PS\) and \(QR\) upwards, we see they intersect at the top point labeled as Point \(Y\). This matches option B.

parts.stem: Construct the diagonals $PR$ and $QS$, at which point do they intersect?

steps.explain: We start by identifying the diagonals of the quadrangle. Diagonals connect opposite vertices: \(PR\) connects \(P\) and \(R\), while \(QS\) connects \(Q\) and \(S\).
Next, we locate the intersection point of these two diagonal lines inside the quadrangle.
Finally, tracing the lines \(PR\) and \(QS\), they cross at the central point labeled as Point \(Z\). This corresponds directly to option C.

parts.stem: Which of the following configurations is NOT mathematically possible for four lines in a plane?
options: Three parallel lines and one concurrent line
Three parallel lines cut by a transversal

steps.explain: We start by reviewing the definitions of parallel and concurrent lines. Parallel lines never meet, whereas concurrent lines are three or more lines that intersect at a single point.

Next, we analyze the statement 'Three parallel lines and one concurrent line'. For a line to be 'concurrent', there must be at least three lines that meet at a point. But since three of the lines are parallel, they can never meet at a point, making this configuration mathematically impossible.

Finally, we verify that four parallel lines (Config A), four concurrent lines (Config F), and three parallel lines cut by a transversal (Config B) are all valid and possible configurations. Thus, Option A is the correct answer.

options: It means there is no limit to the number of points; we can find as many points as we want between any two points.
It means a line has a fixed starting point and an ending point with exactly 10 points.
It means the line contains exactly 100 points.
It means the points are extremely large in size.

steps.explain: We start by analyzing the concept of a line in geometry. A geometric line is continuous and does not consist of discrete, countable steps.
Next, we focus on the word 'infinitely'. In mathematical density, between any two real numbers or points on a line, we can always find another point.
steps.work: \( \text{Density property: } \forall A, B \; \exists C \text{ between } A, B \)

steps.explain: Finally, we conclude that 'infinitely' indicates there is no upper limit or bound to the number of points we can choose. This matches option A.

It means exactly 4 lines can cross at any point.
It means lines are infinitely thick.

questions.stem: What is the definition of a reflex angle?
options: An angle greater than 90° but less than 180°
An angle greater than 180° but less than 360°
An angle greater than 0° but less than 90°
questions.hint: Think of the angle names in order of size: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex, full turn. Where does 'reflex' sit?

steps.explain: Angles have names that depend on their size. Here they are in order from the smallest turn to a full turn (360°).
steps.work: acute < right < obtuse < straight < reflex < full turn

steps.explain: Check each option against the number line.
steps.work: Greater than 90° but less than 180° → ✗ that is an obtuse angle. Exactly 180° → ✗ that is a straight angle. Greater than 0° but less than 90° → ✗ that is an acute angle. Greater than 180° but less than 360° → ✓ reflex.

steps.explain: So the definition of a reflex angle is an angle between 180° and 360°.
steps.work: Reflex angle = more than 180° and less than 360°

keyPoints.note: Reflex is the big angle between a straight line (180°) and a full turn (360°).

parts.stem: The supplement of 136° is ____________
parts.hint: Supplementary angles add up to 180°. What must be added to 136° to make 180°?

steps.explain: 'Supplement' means the angle that makes a total of 180° (a straight line). Supplementary angles add up to 180°.

steps.explain: Subtract the angle you are given from 180°.

steps.explain: Check: 136° + 44° = 180° \(\checkmark\). Common mistakes: 54° is 90° − 36° (mixing up with complementary angles, which add to 90°) and 224° is 360° − 136° (angles round a point).

keyPoints.note: Supplementary angles add to 180°.

parts.stem: Adjacent angles have a common ________ and ________
parts.hint: Adjacent angles sit side by side. What do they share: the corner point and one of the lines.

steps.explain: Adjacent angles are two angles that are NEXT to each other. In the diagram, angle 1 and angle 2 are side by side.

steps.explain: They meet at the same corner point. This point where the arms meet is called the VERTEX.

steps.explain: A protractor is the tool for measuring angles, and a transversal is a line that crosses parallel lines. Neither is shared by adjacent angles.
steps.work: Adjacent angles share a common vertex and a common arm.

keyPoints.note: Adjacent means next to each other.

parts.hint: The arc shows which way the angle is measured. Does it go the short way round or the long way round?

steps.explain: The arc starts at the top arm and travels all the way round the point, almost a full circle, finishing at the other arm. The arrow shows the direction.
steps.work: The marked angle is the <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">long way round</mark>

steps.explain: Check the other names: obtuse is under 180°, straight is exactly 180° and a right angle is 90°. None of them fits an angle that goes almost all the way round.

keyPoints.note: Look at which way the arc is drawn.

keyPoints.note: 360° is a complete turn.

questions.stem: If the probability of landing on yellow is \(1/9\), what is the angle of the yellow sector in a full-turn spinner?
questions.hint: A full turn is 360°. Multiply 360° by the sector’s probability.

keyPoints.note: The sector is 1/9 of a complete revolution.
A complete turn is 360°.

steps.explain: Write the angle as a fraction of a full turn.

questions.stem: Which angle below is closest to a right angle?
questions.hint: A right angle measures 90°. Compare the shaded openings, paying attention to the perpendicular rays in option C.

steps.explain: A right angle is the benchmark for comparison. Its two rays are perpendicular, and its size is 90°.

questions.stem: One shape below has two acute angles and two obtuse angles. Which shape is it?
questions.hint: Check each interior corner against a right angle: acute is less than 90° and obtuse is greater than 90°. A parallelogram has two acute and two obtuse angles when it is not a rectangle.

steps.explain: Use the inside of each quadrilateral when classifying its corners. Acute angles are less than 90°, obtuse angles are greater than 90°, and a right angle is exactly 90°.

keyPoints.note: Check each interior corner against a right angle: acute is less than 90° and obtuse is greater than 90°. A parallelogram has two acute and two obtuse angles when it is not a rectangle.

questions.stem: Hamish builds a skateboard ramp with an incline of approximately 45°. Which of these shows an angle closest to the side view of the incline of the ramp?
questions.hint: A 45° incline is half a right angle. Compare each option’s opening with that benchmark.

steps.explain: The ramp incline is the angle between the horizontal ground and the sloping surface. The target is 45°, half of a right angle.

questions.stem: Which angle is closest in size to 100°?
questions.hint: 100° is 10° greater than a right angle. Find the marked angle that is just obtuse.

steps.explain: A right angle is 90°. An angle closest to 100° is obtuse and only slightly wider than a right angle.

questions.stem: A gymnast does a move where she makes 3 full somersaults and lands back on her feet. By how many degrees has the gymnast rotated her body in this move?
questions.hint: A full turn is 360°. Count the three complete somersaults and multiply by 360°.

steps.explain: One complete somersault brings the gymnast back to the starting orientation, which is one full 360° turn.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 420 155" width="380" height="140" role="img" aria-label="Circular arrows showing complete somersault turns"><rect width="420" height="155" fill="white"/><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0L9 4.5L0 9Z" fill="#7c3aed"/></marker></defs><path d="M109 68 A29 29 0 1 1 52 61" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="80.00" y="73.00" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#7c3aed" >1</text><text x="80.00" y="123.00" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="500" fill="#334155" >1 full turn</text><text x="315.00" y="52.00" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb" >360°</text></svg>

steps.explain: Three somersaults mean three complete turns. Represent this as three equal 360° rotations.

questions.stem: Tom drew this shape on grid paper. Which one of the shapes below when joined to Tom’s shape without an overlap, will not make an isosceles triangle?
questions.hint: Use the grid to compare lengths. An isosceles triangle must have two equal outer sides; check the outline after each piece is joined without overlap.

steps.explain: Count the grid squares along Tom’s two perpendicular sides: each leg is 2 units, so the starting piece is an isosceles right triangle.

questions.stem: Elloise is taking a ride on a ferris wheel. It takes her 5 minutes to complete a full lap. What angle does the Ferris wheel turn through in 75 seconds?
questions.hint: Convert 5 minutes to seconds, then find what fraction of a 300-second lap 75 seconds represents.

steps.explain: One full lap is one complete revolution. First convert the lap time to seconds so both times use the same unit.
Compare the elapsed 75 seconds with the 300-second lap. This is one quarter of a full lap.

steps.explain: A full revolution is 360°. Take one quarter of that turn.

questions.stem: Draw an obtuse angle with your ruler and pencil.
questions.answer: Sample answer: an angle of 125° (any angle greater than 90° and less than 180° is correct).
questions.hint: An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle (90°) but smaller than a straight line (180°). Draw one arm, then use a protractor to mark a point between 91° and 179°.

steps.explain: Recall what 'obtuse' means: bigger than 90° and smaller than 180°. So you may choose any size from 91° to 179°, for example 125°.

questions.hint: The two angles sit side by side on a straight line. What do angles on a straight line add up to?

steps.explain: The diagram is a sketch (not drawn to scale), so use the numbers, not the picture. The ray stands on a straight line.
steps.work: Look for a <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">straight line</mark>: it makes a 180° angle.

steps.explain: The 65° angle and the angle \(x\) are next to each other on the same straight line, so together they make the straight angle.

questions.hint: The two lines with arrows are parallel. Where are the angles x and 95° in relation to the crossing line?

steps.explain: The arrows on the two long lines mean they are PARALLEL. The third line crosses both of them (a transversal). The diagram is not drawn to scale, so use the labels.
steps.work: Parallel lines (amber) cut by a transversal (blue).

parts.stem: What type of angles are the pair of angles marked ♣ and ☺?
parts.hint: Look at the two angles. Do they sit side by side, sharing a corner and an arm?

steps.explain: The ☺ angle is ∠FHG and the ♣ angle is ∠GHJ. Look at where they are.

keyPoints.note: Think about where the two angles sit.

parts.stem: Measure the size of reflex angle FHJ.
parts.hint: A reflex angle is the 'long way round'. Measure the small angle FHJ, then take it away from 360°.

steps.explain: The angle FHJ that is less than 180° is made of the two adjacent angles ∠FHG and ∠GHJ. Measure it with the protractor.

parts.stem: Two angles that sum to 90° are called ____________ angles.
parts.hint: Think: 'complement' completes a right angle (90°). Supplementary angles complete a straight line.

steps.explain: A right angle is 90°. Two angles that together make 90° 'complete' a right angle, as a and b do here.

steps.explain: The word for angles that add up to 90° is COMPLEMENTARY. (Angles that add to 180° are SUPPLEMENTARY.)
Check the other words: cointerior describes angles between parallel lines, perpendicular describes lines that meet at 90°, and a transversal is a line that crosses other lines.

keyPoints.note: Angles that add to 90° are complementary.

meta.source: Year 7 Mathematics Practice · Angles, Perimeter and Area

parts.stem: Adjacent angles share a common ____________ and a common ____________
parts.hint: Adjacent angles are next to each other. They share their corner point and one straight side.

steps.explain: Adjacent angles sit side by side. The corner point where the arms meet is the VERTEX.

steps.explain: They also share one straight side of the angle, which is called an ARM.

steps.explain: A protractor measures angles, a transversal crosses parallel lines and cointerior describes angles between parallel lines. None of these is shared by adjacent angles.

keyPoints.note: Side by side angles.

meta.source: Year 7 Mathematics Practice · Angles, Perimeter and Area

parts.stem: The instrument used to measure an angle is a ____________
parts.hint: It is the half-circle tool with degrees marked round the edge.

steps.explain: To measure angles in degrees we use a half-circle tool with a scale from 0° to 180°.
A protractor is used like this: put its centre mark on the vertex, line its flat edge up with one arm, then read where the other arm crosses the scale.
steps.work: Centre on the <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">vertex</mark>, baseline on one <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">arm</mark>, read the scale.

steps.explain: Check the other words: a transversal is a line, a vertex is a point and an arm is a side of an angle. None of them is an instrument.

keyPoints.note: A tool that measures.

meta.source: Year 7 Mathematics Practice · Angles, Perimeter and Area

parts.stem: A line which cuts two or more parallel lines is a ____________
parts.hint: Picture two parallel lines and one line crossing both of them.

steps.explain: Draw two parallel lines (arrows) and one line that crosses (cuts) both. The crossing line is highlighted.
steps.work: The line that crosses both is the <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">TRANSVERSAL</mark>

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" width="56%" height="auto" style="display:block;margin:0 auto"><line x1="20" y1="60" x2="300" y2="60" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-opacity="1"/><polyline points="292.1,55.8 300,60 292.1,64.2" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="20" y1="140" x2="300" y2="140" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-opacity="1"/><polyline points="292.1,135.8 300,140 292.1,144.2" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="95" y1="185" x2="205" y2="15" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="3.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-opacity="1"/><text x="235" y="32.5" text-anchor="start" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="#92400e">transversal</text></svg>

steps.explain: The word 'transversal' means 'a line that cuts across'. When it crosses two parallel lines it makes eight angles, and these give the angle pairs (corresponding, alternate and co-interior) used to find unknown angles.
steps.work: Transversal = the line that <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">cuts across</mark> the parallel lines.

steps.explain: Perpendicular means meeting at 90° (a transversal may cross at any angle), a protractor is a tool and a vertex is a point.

keyPoints.text: cuts two or more parallel lines
keyPoints.note: The line that crosses the parallel lines.

meta.source: Year 7 Mathematics Practice · Angles, Perimeter and Area

parts.stem: ____________ angles are supplementary between parallel lines.
parts.hint: Supplementary means adding to 180°. Which angles between parallel lines, on the same side of the transversal, add to 180°?

steps.explain: Supplementary means the angles add up to 180°. Look at the two angles a and b: both are between the parallel lines and on the SAME side of the transversal.

steps.explain: These angles are called COINTERIOR angles (also called co-interior or allied angles).
Complementary angles add to 90°, not 180°. Perpendicular and transversal are not names for pairs of angles.
steps.work: Do not mix up COMPLEMENTARY (90°) with SUPPLEMENTARY (180°).

keyPoints.note: Supplementary means the angles add to 180°.

meta.source: Year 7 Mathematics Practice · Angles, Perimeter and Area

parts.stem: Two straight lines that meet at right angles are called ____________ lines.
parts.hint: Right angles are 90° corners.

steps.explain: Two lines that meet at a right angle (90°) make four square corners, shown with the little squares.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 240 180" width="40%" height="auto" style="display:block;margin:0 auto"><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="220" y2="90" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-opacity="1"/><line x1="120" y1="10" x2="120" y2="170" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-opacity="1"/><polyline points="132,90 132,78 120,78" fill="none" fill-opacity="1" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="120,78 108,78 108,90" fill="none" fill-opacity="1" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="108,90 108,102 120,102" fill="none" fill-opacity="1" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="120,102 132,102 132,90" fill="none" fill-opacity="1" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linejoin="round"/></svg>

steps.explain: Each of the four corners is a right angle, so the four angles add up to a full turn.
A transversal crosses parallel lines at any angle, and cointerior and complementary are names for angles, not for lines.

keyPoints.note: A right angle is exactly 90°.

meta.source: Year 7 Mathematics Practice · Angles, Perimeter and Area

questions.stem: In the diagram, AC and DF are cut by transversal BE. The same-side interior angles are 123° and 60°. Explain why AC and DF are not parallel.
options: The interior same-side angles add to 180°.
The interior same-side angles add to 183°, not 180°.
questions.hint: If the lines were parallel, the same-side interior angles would add to 180°. Check the two marked values.

options: Yes, because A + D is more than 180°
No, because A + B = 218°, which is not 180°
Yes, because B + C = 165°, which is less than 180°
No, because A + D = 195°, which is not 180°
questions.hint: If AB and DC are parallel, the angles at A and D (on the same side of AD) must add up to 180°.

steps.explain: Check the sketch first: the four angles of any four-sided shape add to 360°. 120° + 98° + 67° + 75° = 360°, so the figure is possible.
If AB ∥ DC, then AD is a transversal and the angles at A and D (between the parallel lines, on the same side) are co-interior, so they must add to 180°.
